name: Dark Chessylite Blue
lede: Dark Chessylite Blue is a muted, darker modifier on [[chessylite-blue]] — itself named for chessylite, an old name for the mineral azurite — scanned from Ridgway's 1912 plates and filed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955.

sections.title: A mineral's name, twice darkened
sections.body:
The name follows the library's modifier grammar, *dark* plus [[chessylite-blue]], whose own name comes from chessylite, an old mineralogical name for azurite, a copper-carbonate mineral long ground for blue pigment [1]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* records this hue twice, at plate XX, hue 45′ and again at plate XLII, hue 45‴, both scans of aged plates and so only approximate; the ISCC-NBS system filed it in 1955 as a dark greenish blue [1].

Its nearest named neighbors are [[dusky-orient-blue]], almost the same at 2.5 units, and [[pearl-gentian]], at 3.0 [2]. [[connor-s-lakefront|Connor's Lakefront]] sits a little further at 3.5 units, itself one of this color's own nearest neighbors [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color this close to Dark Chessylite Blue is common in our archive: 183 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, about 0.77 percent, more common than 55 percent of the named colors [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 3.5 times the expected rate, and most often sits as a hidden color, 58 percent of the time [3]. The earliest match dates to 1433, by Robert Campin, 479 years before the name's own 1912 record [3]. That is centuries before the name's own record, a floor on the hue's age, not a first use of either the name or a pigment.
